study.title: Jeremiah 23 - Unfaithful Shepherds, liar prophets, and the promise of restoration
study.overview: Jeremiah 23 brings together three great movements: first, the denunciation against leaders who should care for the people, but spread it; then, the severe condemnation of the corrupt prophets and priests, who spoke for themselves and not for God; finally, the exposition of the custom of mocking the prophetic word and the final sentence of lasting shame. In the midst of the denunciation, a decisive hope arises: God himself will gather together the rest of the flock and raise up a righteous king of the lineage of David, who will bring justice, security, and salvation to Judah and Israel.

outline.title: Condemnation of the Shepherds and Promise of a Righteous King
outline.explanation: The text begins with a lament on leaders who have destroyed and dispersed the flock of God. In contrast, the Lord promises to act personally: gather the scattered together, make them return and raise faithful shepherds. The culmination is the promise of the righteous Renewal of David, a king who will do justice and righteousness, and by whom the people will be saved and live in safety.

outline.title: Judgment against corrupt prophets and priests
outline.explanation: Jeremiah describes the devastating effect of false prophecy on himself and on the earth. The prophets and priests are accused of corruption, adultery, falsehood, harm encouragement and invented messages. God rejects those who speak from their hearts, affirm that he has not sent them and declares that his word is not straw, but fire and hammer, able to judge and break hardness.

outline.title: Zombaria with the word of the LORD and final sentence
outline.explanation: The people, along with prophets and priests, treat the divine message by ironicly asking for the "chargae" of the Lord. God commands that this expression no longer be used in this context, because they have perverted their words. The conclusion is a sentence of abandonment, exclusion and perpetual shame over the rebels and the city.

study.context: The chapter dialogues with the leadership crisis in Judah, where kings, prophets and priests appear as responsible for the moral and spiritual ruin of the people. The notes also indicate contrast to the northern kingdom, Samaria, marked by cult of Baal, and point out that Jerusalem was even worse in its corruption. The background includes exile as a confirmed consequence of infidelity, but the text advances to a hope of future restoration.
study.theology: Jeremiah 23 teaches that spiritual authority is not legitimized by office, emotion or appearances, but by fidelity to the word of the LORD. God demands real responsibility from leaders: who should feed and protect and instead dispersed and deceives will be judged. At the same time, the chapter states that God Himself does not definitively abandon his people; he gathers the rest and promises a righteous ruler of David's house. Here is an important theological tension between judgment and grace: the false peace announced by the prophets is dismantled, while true peace comes from the just reign that God Himself establishes. In Protestant evangelical reading, many see in David's Renewal a Messianic reference fulfilled in Christ; this is an interpretation consistent with the chapter, but should be presented as theological reading, not as an explicit definition of the text here in isolation.

scholarViews.insight: The kings of Judah, called figuratively of shepherds, should protect the people; instead they scattered the flock.
The chapter also denounces the desecration of religious discourse, when the people mock the prophets and treats the message of God irreverence.
The judgment on the shepherds includes kings, princes, priests, and prophets who, by evil example and conduct, brought desolation to the people.

questions: What kind of leadership does God reprove in this chapter: only politics, only religious, or both?
How can we distinguish a message from the very heart of a word that comes from the Lord?
How does the promise of David's Renewlement correct the false peace offered by the liar prophets?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to examine two concrete areas. First, any position of influence should be exercised to care, gather and strengthen people, never to disperse or manipulate them. Second, it is necessary to cultivate spiritual discernment: not every religious speech comes from God, and a true message always leads to the abandonment of sin, reverence and obedience. In practice, this means reading Scripture seriously, distrusting easy promises and measuring teachings by fidelity to the character and word of the Lord.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not conclusively detail the exact historical identity of David's Renovo at the very level of the chapter; the Messianic reading is an evangelical theological interpretation, not an explicit statement of the cited text. There is also no data in the notes to accurately enlarge chronologies, specific events of exile beyond the general reference, or exact origin of the technical expressions used in the Portuguese text.
